record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: Can federated learning be extended beyond supervised learning to reinforcement learning, semi-supervised learning, unsupervised learning, active learning, online learning, and Bayesian uncertainty-aware models while preserving scalability and computational feasibility?

evidence.quote: all present interesting and open challenges

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a (potentially very large) set of clients $\{C_1, \ldots, C_N\}$ each holds a private local dataset $D_i$ drawn from a client-specific distribution $\mathcal{P}_i$, and a central coordinator orchestrates the training of a shared model without requiring clients to transmit raw data. A federated training protocol consists of repeated rounds in which a subset of clients perform local computation on their own data and exchange only model updates (or other privacy-preserving summaries) with the coordinator, subject to communication, computation, privacy, and systems heterogeneity constraints.

The standard formulation targets supervised learning, in which each client has labeled examples $(x, y) \sim \mathcal{P}_i$ and the goal is to minimize an aggregate risk $\sum_i w_i \, \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{P}_i}[\ell(f_	heta(x), y)]$ for some loss $\ell$.

Develop federated training protocols, together with rigorous analyses, that extend this framework to each of the following learning paradigms while preserving scalability in the number of clients $N$ and computational feasibility on resource-limited devices:

1. Reinforcement learning, where each client interacts with its own (possibly distinct) Markov decision process and the objective is to learn a shared (or personalized) policy maximizing expected cumulative reward.
2. Semi-supervised learning, where clients hold a mix of labeled and unlabeled data.
3. Unsupervised learning, including representation learning and clustering, where no labels are available.
4. Active learning, where clients can selectively query labels for a limited number of examples.
5. Online learning, where data arrive sequentially at each client and updates must be made on the fly.
6. Bayesian, uncertainty-aware modeling, where the goal is to learn a posterior distribution over model parameters (or predictive uncertainty) rather than a point estimate.

For each paradigm, specify (a) a precise federated objective, (b) a protocol achieving convergence/regret/posterior-approximation guarantees under standard assumptions on client heterogeneity, communication frequency, and privacy budget, and (c) bounds showing that communication, computation, and memory costs scale acceptably as $N$ and the per-client data size grow.
artifact.status_search_result: The extension of federated learning to reinforcement learning, semi-supervised, unsupervised, active, online, and Bayesian uncertainty-aware settings continues to be an active research area, with many partial results (e.g., federated RL frameworks, federated SSL methods such as FedMatch, federated self-supervised learning, federated Bayesian approaches) but no unified solution preserving scalability and feasibility across all paradigms. Recent surveys (2023–2025) still list these as open challenges.

status_evidence.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies extending FL beyond supervised learning (to RL, semi-supervised, unsupervised, active, online, Bayesian) as open challenges.
status_evidence.claim: These extensions are formally posed as open problems.

status_evidence.title: A survey on federated learning: challenges and applications
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys ongoing work in federated RL, semi-supervised FL, and unsupervised FL, noting that scalable solutions remain open.
status_evidence.claim: Recent surveys still treat the cross-paradigm extension as open.
